descripcion: At C2 you handle the rarer reduced forms: a relative clause reduced to a bare noun phrase in apposition, and a participle clause with its own subject (an absolute construction), both markers of dense, highly literate written English.

filas: Maria, who is our lead researcher, confirmed it.
Maria, our lead researcher, confirmed it.
apposition, very common in careful writing
Once the meeting had ended, we left.
The meeting having ended, we left.

ejemplos.texto: Maria, our lead researcher, confirmed the findings personally.
The meeting having ended, the delegates dispersed quickly.
Weather permitting, the launch will proceed as planned.

notas: Apposition (Maria, our lead researcher) drops both the relative pronoun and the verb be entirely — it's extremely common in professional writing and shouldn't be mistaken for an error.
An absolute construction has its own subject, distinct from the main clause's subject — that's what makes it grammatically 'absolute', independent of the rest of the sentence.
Weather permitting and time allowing are fixed absolute constructions worth learning as set phrases.

es.en: Spanish uses apposition in much the same way (María, nuestra investigadora principal), so that device transfers easily. The absolute construction with its own subject is much rarer in Spanish and tends to sound forced if translated literally, so it is best learned as a fixed English pattern.
es.es: El español usa la aposición de manera muy parecida («María, nuestra investigadora principal»), por lo que ese recurso se transfiere fácilmente. La construcción absoluta con sujeto propio es mucho menos frecuente en español y tiende a sonar forzada si se traduce literalmente, por lo que conviene aprenderla como patrón fijo del inglés.

de.en: German knows the absolute construction, but mainly as a literary or fixed form (Den Hut in der Hand, trat er ein; im Büro angekommen, …), so German speakers recognise it but rarely produce it in English. Apposition transfers directly, and is even simpler in English because nothing has to agree in case.
de.de: Deutsch kennt die absolute Konstruktion, vor allem literarisch oder in festen Formen («Den Hut in der Hand, trat er ein»; «im Büro angekommen, …»), daher erkennen Deutschsprachige sie, verwenden sie im Englischen aber selten. Apposition lässt sich direkt übertragen und ist im Englischen sogar einfacher, weil keine Kasusübereinstimmung nötig ist.

it.en: Italian speakers have a real advantage here: the participio assoluto is productive even in everyday writing (Finita la riunione, siamo usciti). The risk is word order, since Italian puts the participle first; English needs the subject first (The meeting over, we left), so Finished the meeting, we left is a typical calque.
it.it: Gli italofoni hanno un vero vantaggio qui: il participio assoluto è produttivo anche nella scrittura quotidiana («Finita la riunione, siamo usciti»). Il rischio è l'ordine delle parole, perché l'italiano mette prima il participio; l'inglese richiede prima il soggetto («The meeting over, we left»), quindi «Finished the meeting, we left» è un calco tipico.

fr.en: French has an almost exact parallel in the participe absolu, with the subject first as in English (La réunion terminée, nous sommes partis – The meeting over, we left). Even fixed forms such as le temps le permettant (weather permitting) exist, so French speakers transfer this construction very easily.
fr.fr: Le français possède un parallèle presque exact avec le participe absolu, sujet placé en premier comme en anglais («La réunion terminée, nous sommes partis» – «The meeting over, we left»). Même des formes figées comme «le temps le permettant» («weather permitting») existent ; cette construction se transfère donc très facilement.

pt.en: Portuguese has both a participle absolute (Terminada a reunião, saímos) and a gerund absolute (Estando o tempo bom, …), so the construction is familiar. As in Italian, the participle comes first, which leads to Finished the meeting, we left instead of The meeting over, we left.
pt.pt: O português tem tanto o particípio absoluto («Terminada a reunião, saímos») quanto o gerúndio absoluto («Estando o tempo bom, …»), então a construção é familiar. Como no italiano, o particípio vem primeiro, o que pode levar a «Finished the meeting, we left» em vez de «The meeting over, we left».

errores: Forgetting the commas around an appositive phrase.
Building an absolute construction where the two subjects are actually the same, which should instead be a simple participle clause.
Using an absolute construction outside formal or literary writing, where it reads as stilted.

redemittel.expresion: That reads as written English, not spoken.
redemittel.funcion: ties the construction to the medium

traducciones.es: Eso se lee como inglés escrito, no hablado.
traducciones.de: Das liest sich wie Schrift-, nicht wie Sprechsprache.
traducciones.fr: Cela se lit comme de l'écrit, pas de l'oral.
traducciones.it: Si legge come scritto, non come parlato.
traducciones.pt: Isso lê-se como escrita, não como fala.

autochequeo: Are commas correctly placed around every appositive phrase?
Does every absolute construction have a subject distinct from the main clause?
Is the absolute construction reserved for formal or literary contexts?
Would a highly literate native reader find this natural, not stilted?
Have I used at least one appositive and one absolute construction?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on apposition and absolute constructions. Check comma placement and whether each absolute construction genuinely has its own subject. Do not rewrite the text.

es: «*Dicho esto*» rendered as *Said this, …* instead of *That said, …*.
de: *vorausgesetzt, dass* rendered as *presupposed that* instead of *provided that*.
it: «*Detto questo*» rendered as *Said this, …* instead of *That said, …*.

pt: *Dito isto* rendered as *Said this, …* instead of *That said, …*.
